caption_hook: Colorado has been a seafloor, a Sahara-style desert and a mountain range that vanished.

layers.name: PIERRE SHALE
layers.hook: Colorado was the bottom of the sea
layers.what: A shallow seaway once split North America in two. Its mud piled up thousands of feet thick and hardened into this shale, packed with ammonites and sea-reptile bones.
layers.bonus: It's also the swelling clay behind cracked basements along the Front Range.

layers.name: DAKOTA SANDSTONE
layers.what: As the seaway crept west, its shoreline left a sheet of tough beach sand. Tilted up by the Rockies, it now stands as the Dakota Hogback ridge west of Denver.
layers.bonus: Dinosaur footprints are still pressed into it at Dinosaur Ridge.

layers.name: MORRISON FORMATION
layers.what: Rivers, swamps and mudflats where the biggest dinosaurs ever lived. In 1877 the first Stegosaurus bones were dug out of this layer near the town of Morrison.
layers.bonus: Stegosaurus is now Colorado's official state fossil.

layers.name: LYONS SANDSTONE
layers.what: Before the dinosaurs, Colorado was a Sahara. Wind-blown dunes turned to stone, and you can still see their sweeping slanted layers in the rock.
layers.bonus: Quarried near Lyons, it gives CU Boulder its pink-red buildings.

layers.name: FOUNTAIN FORMATION
layers.hook: Rubble from a lost mountain range
layers.what: Gravel and sand shed off the Ancestral Rockies, mountains that rose and wore away long before today's Rockies. Tipped on end, it makes the state's most famous red rocks.
layers.bonus: Red Rocks Amphitheatre, the Flatirons and Garden of the Gods are all this one layer.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.what: Below all the layers sits ancient granite and gneiss. Pikes Peak itself is about 1.1-billion-year-old granite, pushed up to 14,115 ft.
layers.bonus: At Manitou Springs, 500-million-year-old sandstone sits right on it: the Great Unconformity, with over half a billion years missing.
